title: Neurulation and Brain Morphogenesis
summary: How the neural plate folds into the neural tube and grows into the brain, spinal cord and neural crest derivatives.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Neurulation

levels.kid:
Imagine a flat piece of playdough on the back of a tiny growing baby. That flat piece is called the **neural plate**. It will become the brain and spinal cord!

First, the edges of the playdough rise up like two little walls. Then they bend toward each other and touch in the middle, making a tube. It is like rolling a flat tortilla into a burrito. This tube is the **neural tube**.

The tube zips closed like a zipper, starting in the middle and moving toward both ends. The very bottom part of the spinal cord is made a different way. Cells bunch into a solid ball and then hollow out inside.

If the zipper does not close, the baby can have a problem with the brain or spine. A vitamin called folic acid helps the zipper close.
levels.hs:
**Neurulation** is the process that turns a flat sheet of cells into the **neural tube**, the structure that becomes the brain and spinal cord. It happens very early, in weeks 3 to 4 after fertilization. Many people do not yet know they are pregnant at this point.

**Primary neurulation** builds most of the tube:
- Signals from the **notochord**, a rod of tissue beneath the ectoderm, tell the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the **neural plate** (day 18 or so).
- The plate's edges rise as **neural folds**, with a **neural groove** between them.
- The folds meet and fuse, first near the future neck region (around day 22). Closure then spreads toward the head and the tail like two zippers.
- The openings at each end are called **neuropores**. The front (cranial) one closes around day 25 and the back (caudal) one around day 28.

**Secondary neurulation** forms the lowest part of the spinal cord, in the sacral and tail region. Here, cells from the **caudal eminence** (tail bud) gather into a solid cord. The cord then hollows out to form a channel that joins the rest of the tube.

When closure fails, the result is a **neural tube defect**. Failure at the head end causes **anencephaly**. Failure lower down causes **spina bifida**. Taking **folic acid** before and during early pregnancy greatly lowers this risk.
levels.college:
Neurulation converts the dorsal ectoderm into the neural tube during weeks 3–4.

**Induction.** The notochord and prechordal mesoderm secrete BMP antagonists: **chordin**, **noggin** and **follistatin**. Ectoderm exposed to BMP4 becomes epidermis. Where BMP signaling is blocked, ectoderm defaults to a neural fate and forms the **neuroectoderm** of the neural plate. FGF signaling also contributes to this step.

**Primary neurulation** has four overlapping stages:
- **Formation** of the neural plate. Cells become tall and columnar.
- **Shaping**. The plate narrows and lengthens through **convergent extension**, a process driven by planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling.
- **Bending**. The plate bends at a **median hinge point** above the notochord and at paired **dorsolateral hinge points**. Cells at the hinges become wedge-shaped through apical actomyosin constriction. Surrounding epidermis and mesoderm also push the plate inward.
- **Closure**. The neural folds meet and fuse dorsally. The neural tube then separates from the surface ectoderm. Neural crest cells delaminate from the fold crests at this point.

In humans, fusion begins at the level of somites 4–6, in the future cervical region, around day 22. It proceeds bidirectionally. The **cranial neuropore** closes around day 25, and the **caudal neuropore** around day 27–28, at roughly the level of somite 31 (upper sacral).

**Secondary neurulation** builds the tube caudal to the caudal neuropore. Mesenchyme of the **caudal eminence** condenses into a solid **medullary cord**. This cord cavitates to form a lumen that becomes continuous with the primary tube. It forms the lower sacral and coccygeal cord, the **conus medullaris** and the **filum terminale**.

The two processes produce different defects:
- Primary failures are **open** defects: anencephaly, craniorachischisis and myelomeningocele.
- Secondary errors give **closed** (skin-covered) dysraphisms, such as a tethered cord or a lipomyelomeningocele.
levels.phd:
Neural induction is no longer viewed as a simple "default model" in which BMP inhibition alone produces neural tissue. In amniotes, FGF and Wnt-inhibitory signals act before gastrulation. BMP antagonists from the organizer (Hensen's node: chordin, noggin, follistatin) then stabilize neural fate. Sox2, Zic and Geminin mark the early neuroectoderm.

**Convergent extension** depends on the non-canonical Wnt/PCP pathway: Vangl2, Celsr1, Frizzled, Dishevelled and Scribble. In the *loop-tail* mouse (a *Vangl2* mutation), the neural plate stays too wide. The folds cannot meet, causing **craniorachischisis**. This is the most severe NTD, with the tube open from midbrain to spine. Rare *VANGL1/2* and *CELSR1* variants occur in human NTD cohorts.

The mouse literature defines three closure modes along the spinal axis:
- Mode 1: median hinge point only (upper spine).
- Mode 2: median plus dorsolateral hinge points.
- Mode 3: dorsolateral hinge points only (low spine).

The dorsolateral hinge points are regulated by opposing signals. Sonic hedgehog from the notochord inhibits them. **Noggin** from the dorsal fold tips promotes them. Mice also have several closure initiation sites. Closure 2, at the forebrain–midbrain boundary, is strain-variable. The existence of discrete human sites (the "multisite closure" hypothesis of Van Allen and colleagues) remains debated.

Fold fusion involves surface-ectoderm protrusions, ephrin–Eph interactions and grainyhead-like transcription factors (Grhl2/3). The *curly tail* mouse (*Grhl3* hypomorph) develops spina bifida because of a cell-proliferation imbalance. These lesions are notably resistant to folate but respond to inositol.

**Secondary neurulation** in humans and mice arises from **neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs)** in the tail bud. NMPs co-express Sox2 and T/Brachyury. Their choice between a neural and a mesodermal fate depends on the balance of Wnt and FGF signals versus retinoic acid. This shared bipotent origin explains why caudal dysraphisms often coexist with vertebral, anorectal and urogenital anomalies.

The MRC Vitamin Study (1991) showed that periconceptional folic acid prevented about 72% of recurrent NTDs. Mandatory food fortification later lowered NTD prevalence in the US and Canada. Not all NTDs are folate-sensitive, however. Folate's mechanism (nucleotide synthesis versus methylation) remains unresolved.
levels.expert:
For a neurosurgeon, neurulation biology maps directly onto how patients are sorted for care. **Open spinal dysraphisms** arise from failed primary closure. They expose neural placode to amniotic fluid and include myelomeningocele (MMC) and myelocele. MMC is now often diagnosed at the mid-trimester scan. Ultrasound may show the "lemon" sign (scalloped frontal bones) and the "banana" sign (a curved cerebellum). These findings reflect **Chiari II malformation**, caused by CSF leaking from the open defect and leaving the posterior fossa underexpanded. Maternal serum AFP is often raised.

The **two-hit hypothesis** holds that damage results from the primary malformation plus secondary amniotic and mechanical injury in utero. This idea motivated the **MOMS trial** (2011), in which prenatal repair before 26 weeks:
- reduced shunt-dependent hydrocephalus (roughly 40% vs 82%),
- reversed hindbrain herniation in many fetuses,
- improved motor outcomes at 30 months.

The costs were higher rates of preterm birth and uterine dehiscence. Fetoscopic approaches aim to cut maternal morbidity, and comparative outcomes are still being collected.

**Closed (occult) dysraphisms** usually reflect errors of secondary neurulation or of disjunction. They include lipomyelomeningocele, fatty filum, terminal myelocystocele, split cord malformation and dermal sinus tracts. Cutaneous markers should prompt imaging:
- lumbosacral hairy patch,
- capillary hemangioma,
- atypical or high dimples,
- subcutaneous lipoma.

In infancy, spinal ultrasound is possible while the posterior elements remain unossified. MRI is definitive. A **tethered cord** has a low-lying conus, below L2–L3 after infancy. It can cause progressive bladder dysfunction, foot deformity, scoliosis and back pain as the child grows. Untethering aims to halt decline rather than reverse it.

From a pharmacology angle, some antiseizure drugs, especially **valproate** and to a lesser extent **carbamazepine**, are recognized NTD teratogens. Pregestational diabetes and maternal obesity also raise risk. Closure is finished by day 28, before many pregnancies are recognized. This timing is why preconception counselling and food fortification matter more than treatment started after pregnancy is detected.

Open questions remain:
- why folate-resistant NTDs persist,
- how gene–environment interactions combine,
- whether inositol supplementation helps humans, which is under trial,
- how human embryo-like models (stem-cell-derived neural tube organoids) can expose human-specific closure mechanics.

keyPoints: Neurulation forms the neural tube in weeks 3–4
Notochord BMP antagonists (chordin, noggin) induce the neural plate
Primary neurulation: plate folds and fuses; neuropores close ~days 25 and 28
Secondary neurulation: tail-bud cord cavitates to form lower sacral cord
Failed primary closure gives open defects like anencephaly and myelomeningocele
Periconceptional folic acid greatly reduces neural tube defect risk

test.q: Which structure induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate?
test.explain: The notochord secretes BMP antagonists that make the overlying ectoderm become neural.

test.q: Where does neural tube fusion first begin in humans?
test.explain: Fusion starts near somites 4–6, in the future neck region. It then zips toward the head and the tail.

test.q: Roughly when does the caudal neuropore close?
test.explain: The caudal neuropore closes around days 27–28, a few days after the cranial neuropore closes at about day 25.

test.q: Failure of the cranial neuropore to close produces:
test.explain: Anencephaly results from failed cranial closure. Spina bifida results from failed closure lower down the spine.

test.q: Secondary neurulation forms a tube by:
test.explain: Caudal eminence cells condense into a solid medullary cord, which then cavitates to form a lumen.

test.q: BMP antagonists such as chordin and noggin act on ectoderm by:
test.explain: BMP4 pushes ectoderm toward an epidermal fate. Blocking BMP lets the ectoderm become neural instead.

test.q: Wedge-shaped cells at hinge points form mainly through:
test.explain: Constriction of the apical actomyosin network narrows the cell tops into wedges, which bends the plate.

test.q: Defects arising from secondary neurulation are typically:
test.explain: Errors of secondary neurulation give closed, skin-covered dysraphisms, such as tethered cord.

test.q: The narrowing and lengthening of the neural plate is called:
test.explain: Convergent extension, driven by planar cell polarity signaling, shapes the plate.

test.q: Which B vitamin taken around conception lowers neural tube defect risk?
test.explain: Periconceptional folic acid prevents a large share of neural tube defects.

test.q: The openings at each end of the closing neural tube are called ___.
test.explain: There is a cranial neuropore at the head end and a caudal neuropore at the tail end.

test.q: Secondary neurulation arises from the caudal ___, also called the tail bud.
test.explain: The caudal eminence supplies the cells that form the lowest part of the spinal cord.

kidTest.q: What does the neural tube become?
kidTest.explain: The neural tube grows into the brain and spinal cord.

kidTest.q: How does the flat neural plate become a tube?
kidTest.explain: The edges rise up, bend toward each other and close, like rolling a burrito.

kidTest.q: How is the very bottom of the spinal cord made?
kidTest.explain: Cells bunch into a solid ball and then hollow out inside.

kidTest.q: Which vitamin helps the tube close?
kidTest.explain: Folic acid helps the neural tube zip shut.

kidTest.q: The neural tube closes like a z _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Closure moves along the tube like a zipper.

advancedTest.q: A Vangl2 mutant mouse has a neural plate that stays wide, and its folds fail to meet along the whole axis. The best explanation is:
choices: Overactive Shh promoting the dorsolateral hinge points
Failed planar cell polarity disrupting convergent extension
Excess folate blocking nucleotide synthesis in the plate
Loss of Grhl3 reducing proliferation in the hindgut
advancedTest.explain: Loss of PCP signaling prevents convergent extension. The plate stays too wide for the folds to meet, which causes craniorachischisis.

advancedTest.q: Why are caudal dysraphisms often accompanied by vertebral and anorectal anomalies?
choices: The caudal neuropore closes before the cranial one
Folate deficiency mainly targets caudal tissues
Neural and mesodermal tissue share tail-bud progenitors
Chiari II malformation spreads defects downward
advancedTest.explain: Neuromesodermal progenitors give rise to both the caudal neural tube and the mesoderm, so a single disruption can affect both.

advancedTest.q: The MOMS trial rationale for prenatal myelomeningocele repair rests mainly on:
choices: Reopening the neuropore so it can close normally
Limiting secondary in utero injury to the exposed tissue
Inducing secondary neurulation to replace the placode
Raising maternal folate levels during the repair
advancedTest.explain: The two-hit hypothesis holds that amniotic and mechanical exposure adds injury after the primary defect. Early repair limits that second hit.

advancedTest.q: Why does preconception folate matter more than folate started once pregnancy is detected?
choices: Folate is poorly absorbed late in pregnancy
Neural tube closure ends around day 28
Folate acts mainly on placental growth
advancedTest.explain: Closure is complete by about day 28, often before pregnancy is recognized, so folate must already be present.

lessons.title: Brain Vesicles, Flexures and Ventricular System Origins

levels.kid:
Early in a baby's growth, the brain starts as a soft tube, like a long balloon filled with water.

The front end of the tube puffs out into **three bubbles**. Later, two of those bubbles split again, so there are **five bubbles**. Each bubble grows into a different part of the brain. One becomes the thinking brain, and one becomes the part that connects to the spinal cord.

The tube also **bends**, like a drinking straw folded to fit in a small box. That is how a big brain fits inside a small head.

The hollow space inside the tube never goes away. It becomes little rooms full of clear liquid called **ventricles**. The liquid helps cushion and feed the brain.
levels.hs:
After the neural tube closes (around day 28 of development), its front end grows much faster than the rest. It swells into **brain vesicles**, which are fluid-filled bulges.

By week 4 there are three **primary vesicles**:
- **Prosencephalon** (forebrain)
- **Mesencephalon** (midbrain)
- **Rhombencephalon** (hindbrain)

By week 5 these become five **secondary vesicles**. The forebrain splits into the **telencephalon** (future cerebral hemispheres) and **diencephalon** (thalamus and hypothalamus). The midbrain stays as the mesencephalon. The hindbrain splits into the **metencephalon** (pons and cerebellum) and **myelencephalon** (medulla).

Because the brain grows faster than the head around it, the tube bends at **flexures**. The **cephalic (midbrain) flexure** and the **cervical flexure** bend the tube forward. The **pontine flexure** bends the opposite way and spreads open the roof of the hindbrain.

The hollow center, or **lumen**, becomes the **ventricular system**, which is filled with **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**. Each vesicle has its own part. For example, the telencephalon's cavity becomes the two **lateral ventricles**, and the narrow midbrain cavity becomes the **cerebral aqueduct**. If the aqueduct is blocked, fluid builds up. This condition, called **hydrocephalus**, is one reason neurosurgeons place shunts in babies.
levels.college:
Rostral neural tube growth produces a sequence of vesicles. Each vesicle maps onto adult structures and a ventricular compartment:

- **Telencephalon**: cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, hippocampus, olfactory bulbs. Its cavity becomes the **lateral ventricles**.
- **Diencephalon**: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (pineal), neurohypophysis, and the optic vesicles, so the **retina** is diencephalic. Its cavity becomes the **third ventricle**.
- **Mesencephalon**: tectum (superior and inferior colliculi), tegmentum, cerebral peduncles. Its cavity becomes the **cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)**.
- **Metencephalon**: pons and cerebellum. Its cavity becomes the upper **fourth ventricle**.
- **Myelencephalon**: medulla. Its cavity becomes the lower fourth ventricle, which is continuous with the spinal **central canal**.

The lateral ventricles connect to the third ventricle through the **interventricular foramina (of Monro)**.

**Flexures.** The **cephalic (mesencephalic) flexure** appears first and is ventral; it persists as the angle between brainstem and forebrain. The **cervical flexure** is ventral, at the hindbrain-spinal cord junction. The **pontine flexure** is dorsal and divides the rhombencephalon. It pushes the alar plates laterally like an opened book, which thins the hindbrain roof into a membrane over a diamond-shaped **rhomboid fossa**, the floor of the fourth ventricle.

**Ventricles and CSF.** When the neural tube closes, its lumen is briefly sealed. Fluid pressure inside the closed lumen helps drive vesicle expansion. **Choroid plexuses** form where vascular pia mater invaginates the thin roof plate (**tela choroidea**) of the fourth, third and lateral ventricles, and they begin producing CSF. Late in the embryonic period the fourth ventricle roof opens at the median aperture (**foramen of Magendie**) and the two lateral apertures (**foramina of Luschka**). These openings let CSF reach the subarachnoid space.

The aqueduct is the narrowest point, making **aqueductal stenosis** a classic cause of congenital obstructive hydrocephalus.
levels.phd:
Vesicle formation reflects regionalized proliferation and hydrostatic expansion under the control of secondary organizers. Desmond and Jacobson's classic chick experiments showed that occluding the spinal neural canal causes brain-cavity pressure to rise, and that draining embryonic CSF (eCSF) collapses the vesicles and reduces growth. Transient occlusion of the neurocoel is therefore an active morphogenetic step. eCSF is protein-rich, carrying factors such as FGF2, IGF2, retinol-binding protein and lipoproteins. Explant work (Gato and colleagues; Lehtinen et al., 2011 for IGF2) indicates that eCSF supports neuroepithelial proliferation and survival.

Boundaries between vesicles align with organizer centers. The **isthmic organizer** at the midbrain-hindbrain boundary is positioned by mutual repression between **Otx2** (rostral) and **Gbx2** (caudal). It secretes **FGF8** and Wnt1, maintains the En1/2 and Pax2/5 domains, and specifies tectum and cerebellum. Transplanting the isthmus induces ectopic midbrain or cerebellar tissue (Martinez, Alvarado-Mallart). The **zona limitans intrathalamica**, a Shh-secreting spike, subdivides the diencephalon. The **anterior neural ridge** (FGF8) patterns the telencephalon.

The prosomeric model (Puelles and Rubenstein) reframes vesicles as neuromeres along a curved longitudinal axis that follows the flexures. In this model the hypothalamus is rostral to, not below, the thalamus, and the classical "diencephalon" is split into hypothalamo-telencephalic and diencephalic prosomeres p1-p3. The hindbrain shows transient **rhombomeres** (r1-r8), compartments with lineage restriction (Fraser, Keynes and Lumsden, 1990) and Hox-coded identities. r1 lacks Hox expression and generates the cerebellum.

Flexure mechanics remain debated. Proposed contributors include differential proliferation, notochord and ventral midline constraints, cardiac and pharyngeal growth, and tension generated by eCSF pressure. Finite-element and surgical studies by Taber and colleagues suggest that the cephalic flexure needs both intrinsic bending and extrinsic forces.

The telencephalic vesicles expand dorsolaterally and caudally, then curve forward into a C shape around the insula. This explains why the lateral ventricle, caudate and fornix are all C-shaped and why the temporal horn lies inferolaterally.
levels.expert:
Clinically, vesicle and ventricular development link directly to several neurosurgical problems.

**Holoprosencephaly** results from failed prosencephalic cleavage, with a monoventricle and fused thalami in the alobar form. It is associated with **SHH**, ZIC2, SIX3 and TGIF1 variants, trisomy 13 and maternal diabetes. Cholesterol is required for Shh processing and signaling. That link explains HPE features in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome and the cyclopia caused by the Veratrum alkaloid **cyclopamine**, which acts as a Smoothened antagonist. This science later led to Smoothened inhibitors (vismodegib, sonidegib) for basal cell carcinoma, a striking path from teratology to oncology.

**Congenital hydrocephalus** sorts into obstructive and communicating types. X-linked aqueductal stenosis (**L1CAM**) is the archetype. Newer exome studies (Kahle, Jin and colleagues) implicate genes such as TRIM71, SMARCC1 and PTCH1 in neuroepithelial and neural stem cell biology. This work reframes some "plumbing" hydrocephalus as a primary disorder of brain development, which may explain persistent neurodevelopmental deficits after successful CSF diversion. **Ependymal ciliopathies** (FOXJ1 variants, primary ciliary dyskinesia) disrupt coordinated CSF flow.

**Hindbrain malformations**: **Dandy-Walker malformation** combines cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle with vermian hypoplasia and an upward-displaced torcula. It is attributed to abnormal roof development and delayed Magendie opening, with FOXC1 and ZIC1/4 involvement. **Chiari II** arises secondarily from open myelomeningocele. The leaking CSF fails to distend the rhombencephalic vesicle, so the posterior fossa forms small, which is McLone's unified theory. The fetal MOMS trial (2011) showed prenatal repair reduced the need for shunting and the degree of hindbrain herniation.

**Pitfalls**: in fetal MRI a cavum septi pellucidi and physiologically prominent ventricles are normal. Ventriculomegaly is defined as an atrial width of 10 mm or more, and isolated mild cases often have good outcomes. On ultrasound, a normal open fourth ventricle seen early can mimic a Blake's pouch cyst.

Treatment choices follow the anatomy. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy, often combined with choroid plexus cauterization (Warf), bypasses aqueductal obstruction, and its success depends on age and etiology. Open questions include how eCSF composition regulates progenitor pools in humans and whether organoids, which lack physiological lumen pressure, faithfully model vesicle growth.

keyPoints: Three primary vesicles: prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon
Five secondary vesicles: tel-, di-, mes-, met-, myelencephalon
Cephalic and cervical flexures bend ventrally; the pontine flexure bends dorsally
Pontine flexure opens the hindbrain into the rhomboid fossa (4th ventricle floor)
Neural tube lumen becomes lateral, 3rd and 4th ventricles, aqueduct and central canal
Aqueductal stenosis is a classic cause of congenital hydrocephalus

test.q: Which primary vesicle divides into the telencephalon and diencephalon?
test.explain: The prosencephalon (forebrain) splits into telencephalon and diencephalon. The rhombencephalon gives the metencephalon and myelencephalon.

test.q: The cerebellum and pons develop from which secondary vesicle?
test.explain: The metencephalon forms the pons and cerebellum. The myelencephalon forms the medulla.

test.q: The cavity of the mesencephalon becomes the:
test.explain: The narrow midbrain lumen becomes the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius.

test.q: The retina is derived from which brain vesicle?
test.explain: The optic vesicles grow out from the diencephalon, so the retina is diencephalic tissue.

test.q: Which flexure bends dorsally and opens the hindbrain roof?
test.explain: The pontine flexure bends in the opposite direction to the others. It spreads the alar plates apart and thins the roof over the fourth ventricle.

test.q: The lateral ventricles connect to the third ventricle through the:
test.explain: The interventricular foramina of Monro connect the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle. The cerebral aqueduct links the third and fourth ventricles, and the foramina of Luschka and Magendie open the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

test.q: Why is aqueductal stenosis a classic cause of congenital hydrocephalus?
choices: The aqueduct drains blood from the brain
The aqueduct is the narrowest ventricular passage
The aqueduct lacks any ependymal lining
The aqueduct produces most of the CSF
test.explain: The aqueduct is the narrowest point of the system, so narrowing there blocks CSF flow. CSF is made mainly by the choroid plexus.

test.q: Choroid plexuses form where:
choices: Dura mater folds into the brain surface
Pia mater invaginates a thin ventricular roof
Neural crest cells line the spinal canal
Ependyma thickens over the basal plates
test.explain: Vascular pia mater pushes into the thin roof plate (tela choroidea), forming CSF-producing choroid plexus.

test.q: The diamond-shaped floor of the fourth ventricle is called the:
test.explain: The opened hindbrain floor forms the rhomboid fossa.

test.q: Name the secondary vesicle that becomes the medulla.
test.explain: The myelencephalon is the caudal hindbrain vesicle, continuous with the spinal cord.

test.q: The clear liquid filling the ventricles is called cerebrospinal ___.
test.explain: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cushions the brain and is produced mainly by the choroid plexus.

test.q: What term describes excess CSF buildup within the ventricles?
test.explain: Hydrocephalus is often treated with shunts or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

kidTest.q: What does the brain start out as?
kidTest.explain: The brain begins as the front part of a hollow tube.

kidTest.q: How many bubbles does the front of the tube make first?
kidTest.explain: First there are three bubbles, which later become five.

kidTest.q: Why does the brain tube bend?
choices: To fit inside a small head
kidTest.explain: Bending lets a big brain fit inside a small space.

kidTest.q: What fills the ventricles?
kidTest.explain: Ventricles are filled with clear fluid that cushions the brain.

kidTest.q: The fluid-filled rooms inside the brain are called v _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The hollow inside of the tube becomes the ventricles.

advancedTest.q: In chick embryos, draining embryonic CSF causes the brain vesicles to collapse and grow less. This best supports which idea?
choices: Choroid plexus is required for neural tube closure
Luminal fluid pressure helps drive vesicle expansion
Flexures form from cardiac growth alone
advancedTest.explain: Desmond and Jacobson showed that a sealed, pressurized neurocoel promotes expansion. Removing the fluid removes that force.

advancedTest.q: Transplanting the midbrain-hindbrain boundary induces ectopic tectum or cerebellum. Which signal is central to this effect?
advancedTest.explain: The isthmic organizer, positioned by the Otx2/Gbx2 boundary, secretes FGF8 that patterns the midbrain and cerebellum.

advancedTest.q: Why does McLone's unified theory link open myelomeningocele to a small posterior fossa in Chiari II?
choices: The aqueduct opens too early in the fetus
Leaked CSF fails to distend the hindbrain vesicle
advancedTest.explain: CSF leakage through the open defect lowers luminal pressure, so the rhombencephalic vesicle and the posterior fossa around it stay small.

advancedTest.q: Cyclopamine causes holoprosencephaly and also inspired cancer drugs. What shared mechanism links these?
choices: Blocking FGF8 receptors at the isthmic organizer
Disrupting L1CAM adhesion in the aqueduct wall
Activating Wnt1 signaling in the midbrain tectum
advancedTest.explain: Cyclopamine antagonizes Smoothened, which blocks Shh-driven forebrain cleavage. Smoothened inhibitors such as vismodegib exploit the same target in basal cell carcinoma.

lessons.title: Dorsoventral Patterning of the Spinal Cord: Alar and Basal Plates

levels.kid:
Imagine a tube of toothpaste standing up inside your back. That tube is the baby's growing spinal cord. Its back side and its front side get very different jobs.

The back side becomes the **feeling** part. It listens for messages like "ouch, that's hot!" coming from the skin.

The front side becomes the **moving** part. It sends messages to muscles saying "pull your hand away!"

How does each cell know which side it is on? Helper cells at the front and back give off special chemical signals, a bit like smells. A cell near the front smells a lot of the front signal and becomes a moving cell. A cell near the back becomes a feeling cell.
levels.hs:
After the neural tube closes, its wall thickens into layers of dividing cells. A shallow groove on each inner side, the **sulcus limitans**, splits each side wall into two regions:

- The **alar plate** (dorsal, toward the back) becomes the **dorsal horn**, which handles sensory information such as touch, pain and temperature.
- The **basal plate** (ventral, toward the belly) becomes the **ventral horn**, which holds **motor neurons** that control skeletal muscle.

The thin midline strips are the **roof plate** (top) and **floor plate** (bottom).

What tells cells where they are? Signaling molecules called **morphogens** spread out from sources and form gradients:
- The **notochord**, a rod under the neural tube, and then the floor plate release **Sonic hedgehog (Shh)**, which ventralizes the tube.
- The overlying ectoderm and the roof plate release **BMPs** and **Wnts**, which dorsalize it.

A cell reads how much of each signal it receives and switches on matching genes. Example: if the notochord is removed from a chick embryo, the floor plate and motor neurons fail to form. This shows that Shh from below is needed to make the 'motor' side.

In the thoracic and upper lumbar cord, a small **intermediate horn** forms near the sulcus limitans. It holds autonomic (sympathetic) neurons.
levels.college:
The spinal cord's dorsoventral (DV) organization is set up during and just after neurulation by opposing morphogen gradients acting on the neuroepithelium.

**Anatomy of the patterned tube.** The ventricular (proliferative) zone produces neuroblasts that migrate into the **mantle layer** (future gray matter). Axons fill the outer **marginal layer** (future white matter). The **sulcus limitans** separates:
- **Alar plate**: dorsal horn interneurons that relay somatic and visceral sensation. Primary sensory neuron cell bodies do not sit here. They sit in dorsal root ganglia, which come from neural crest.
- **Basal plate**: somatic motor neurons of the ventral horn. In T1 to L2 (plus S2 to S4 for parasympathetic output), preganglionic visceral motor neurons sit in the lateral or intermediolateral column.
- **Roof and floor plates**: non-neuronal signaling centers that later become largely ependymal.

**Ventral signaling.** The notochord secretes **Shh**. This induces the floor plate, which then makes Shh itself, a homeogenetic relay. The resulting ventral-to-dorsal Shh gradient is read through Patched/Smoothened and **Gli** transcription factors.

**Dorsal signaling.** Surface ectoderm and then the roof plate secrete **BMP4/7, GDF7 and Wnt1/3a**. These pattern six dorsal interneuron classes (dI1 to dI6), with dI1 to dI3 depending most strongly on roof plate signals.

**Transcriptional code.** Shh represses **Class I** homeodomain genes (Pax6, Pax7, Irx3, Dbx1/2) and induces **Class II** genes (Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, Olig2). Pairs of these factors repress each other, which sharpens the gradient into discrete progenitor domains: p0, p1, p2, pMN and p3. These give rise to V0 to V3 interneurons and motor neurons. **Olig2** marks the pMN domain. That domain later switches to making oligodendrocytes.

**Clinical link.** Defects in dorsal or ventral identity are rare. However, loss of motor neurons in **spinal muscular atrophy**, and the pattern of deficits after cord lesions, both reflect this alar/basal division. That division explains sensory versus motor loss.
levels.phd:
DV patterning of the spinal cord is a textbook example of positional information. It is transformed into discrete cell fates through a gene regulatory network (GRN), not read out by simple concentration thresholds.

**Shh gradient and its interpretation.** Jessell's group (Roelink, Ericson, Briscoe) showed in the 1990s that graded Shh concentrations induce distinct ventral identities in neural plate explants, with progressively higher levels needed for more ventral fates. In vivo, Shh is lipid-modified (cholesterol and palmitate), which shapes its range. Its spread is further governed by Dispatched, Scube2, and the co-receptors Cdon/Boc/Gas1, while induced Patched1 sequesters the ligand. Gli activators (Gli2 primarily) and Gli3 repressor read the signal in a primary-cilium-dependent process.

**Temporal adaptation.** Dessaud, Briscoe and colleagues (2007) showed that cells integrate both the **concentration and the duration** of Shh exposure. Progenitors become desensitized over time as Ptch1 is upregulated. Sustained signaling is needed to reach the Nkx2.2 (p3) state.

**GRN dynamics.** Cross-repression among Pax6, Olig2, Nkx2.2 and Irx3 creates multistable switches with hysteresis. Balaskas et al. (2012) showed that this network turns a noisy, changing gradient into sharp, reproducible boundaries. Domains can also scale with tissue size, a point still under active study.

**Dorsal patterning.** BMP and Wnt signals from the roof plate specify dI1 to dI3, and the bHLH factors Atoh1 (dI1), Ngn1/2 and Ascl1 subdivide these classes. Lmx1b and Tlx3 versus Pax2 later separate glutamatergic from GABAergic dorsal horn fates (dILB versus dILA). Lee, Dietrich and Jessell (2000) showed that genetically ablating the roof plate (via Gdf7-driven diphtheria toxin) removes dI1 to dI3 neurons.

**Sulcus limitans in context.** This classical His boundary roughly corresponds to the transition between Pax7-positive (dorsal) and Pax7-negative domains. It is a morphological correlate of an underlying molecular boundary, not the boundary itself.

**Controversy.** It is still debated how much of patterning depends on morphogen gradients versus mechanical forces and tissue growth (Kicheva et al., 2014). Pure French-flag models are now seen as incomplete.
levels.expert:
For clinicians, DV patterning explains why spinal cord pathology produces dissociated sensory and motor syndromes. It is also the blueprint behind stem-cell-derived therapies.

**Clinical anatomy rooted in development.**
- **Anterior cord syndrome** (anterior spinal artery infarct) damages basal-plate derivatives (ventral horn and corticospinal tracts) plus spinothalamic fibers. Dorsal column function is spared.
- **Spinal muscular atrophy** (SMN1 loss) and **ALS** selectively hit pMN-derived lower motor neurons. Nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide that modifies SMN2 splicing, and onasemnogene abeparvovec gene therapy changed SMA's natural history and made newborn screening a priority.
- **Syringomyelia** often first destroys decussating spinothalamic fibers near the central canal, producing a cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation.

**Hedgehog pathway in disease.** Germline variants in SHH, GLI2 and PTCH1 cause holoprosencephaly-spectrum disorders. Ciliopathies (Joubert syndrome, Meckel-Gruber) disturb Gli processing and DV patterning. Cholesterol-synthesis defects (Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome) and teratogens that inhibit Smoothened (cyclopamine, from Veratrum) show how Shh lipidation and signaling matter. Smoothened inhibitors such as vismodegib and sonidegib, used for basal cell carcinoma and SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma, carry embryo-fetal toxicity warnings for exactly this reason.

**Directed differentiation.** Wichterle and colleagues (2002) recapitulated development in a dish: retinoic acid (caudalization) plus Hedgehog agonism (ventralization) converted mouse embryonic stem cells into motor neurons. Human iPSC-derived motor neurons and Olig2-lineage oligodendrocyte progenitors are now used for ALS disease modelling, drug screening and remyelination trials in spinal cord injury. Their efficacy so far is modest.

**Pitfalls.**
- Mislabeling dorsal root ganglion neurons as alar plate derivatives is a common mistake. They come from neural crest.
- Patterning in the hindbrain and midbrain differs. There, cranial nerve nuclei form functional columns that are partly displaced. Rhombomere-specific Hox codes also apply.

**Open questions.** How do domain sizes scale across species and with growth? How much do mechanical forces contribute to patterning? How do human-specific timing differences, now studied in neural tube organoids and stembryos, shape outcomes? Can these differences be exploited to generate specific interneuron classes for circuit repair?

keyPoints: The sulcus limitans divides the neural tube wall into a dorsal alar plate and a ventral basal plate
Alar plate forms dorsal horn sensory interneurons; basal plate forms ventral horn motor neurons
Notochord and floor plate secrete Sonic hedgehog to ventralize the tube
Roof plate BMPs and Wnts dorsalize the tube and specify dorsal interneurons
Cross-repressing transcription factors (Pax6, Olig2, Nkx2.2) create discrete progenitor domains
Cells read both the concentration and duration of Shh signaling

lessons.title: Neural Crest Cells and Their Many Derivatives

levels.kid:
When a baby is just starting to grow, a groove on its back rolls up into a tube. That tube will become the brain and spinal cord.

Right at the edges of the tube, a special group of cells lets go and goes exploring. These are called **neural crest cells**. They are like travelers leaving home on a long trip.

They crawl all over the growing body. Where they stop, they turn into new things:
- The color in your skin and hair
- The nerves that make you feel touch
- Bones in your face and jaw
- Nerves that help your tummy move food along

That is why scientists call them amazing. One small group of cells helps build lots of different parts of you!
levels.hs:
During **neurulation**, the flat neural plate folds up and its edges meet to form the **neural tube**. Cells at the very edge of the folds, the border between the neural plate and the future skin (**ectoderm**), become **neural crest cells**.

Neural crest cells do something unusual. They undergo an **epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)**. That means they stop being tightly glued sheet cells and become loose, crawling cells. Then they **migrate** along set paths through the embryo.

Their many derivatives include:
- **Melanocytes**, the pigment cells of skin and hair
- **Sensory neurons** of the dorsal root ganglia
- **Autonomic neurons**, including the enteric nervous system of the gut
- **Schwann cells**, which wrap peripheral nerves in myelin
- **Adrenal medulla** cells, which release adrenaline
- Bone, cartilage and connective tissue of the **face and skull**

Because they form so many tissue types, some scientists call the neural crest the "fourth germ layer."

A real example: in **Hirschsprung disease**, neural crest cells fail to migrate all the way down the large intestine. The last part of the colon has no nerve cells to push stool along. Babies can become severely constipated and need surgery to remove that segment.
levels.college:
Neural crest cells arise at the **neural plate border**, between neural and non-neural ectoderm. The border is specified by intermediate **BMP** signaling together with **Wnt** and **FGF** signals. These signals induce border genes (**Pax3/7, Msx1, Zic1**) and then neural crest specifiers (**Snail2/Slug, FoxD3, Sox9, Sox10**).

**Delamination.** Crest cells undergo EMT. They downregulate **E-cadherin** and N-cadherin, switch to cadherins such as cadherin-7, and degrade basal lamina. In mammals, cranial crest leaves before the folds fuse, while trunk crest leaves after tube closure.

**Axial populations and derivatives:**
- **Cranial**: craniofacial bone and cartilage (ectomesenchyme), odontoblasts, cranial nerve ganglia (with placodes), and the parafollicular C cells via the pharyngeal arches.
- **Cardiac**: the **aorticopulmonary septum** and conotruncal cushions.
- **Vagal and sacral**: the **enteric nervous system**.
- **Trunk**: dorsal root ganglia, sympathetic chain ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla chromaffin cells and melanocytes.

**Migration routes (trunk).** The **ventral pathway** passes through the anterior half of each somite's sclerotome. It forms the DRG, sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. Posterior-half **ephrins** and **semaphorins** repel crest cells, and this segments the ganglia. The **dorsolateral pathway** runs between the dermomyotome and ectoderm and carries melanoblasts. In the trunk, melanoblasts take this route after the ventral wave.

**Neurocristopathies** are disorders of the neural crest:
- **Hirschsprung disease**: mutations in RET, EDNRB or EDN3.
- **Waardenburg syndrome**: PAX3, MITF or SOX10. It causes pigment defects and deafness.
- **DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion)**: it combines conotruncal heart defects, thymic and parathyroid problems, and facial anomalies.
- **Treacher Collins syndrome**
- **Neuroblastoma**

The trunk crest normally does not make skeleton, but cranial crest does. This reflects differences in Hox gene expression: anterior cranial crest is Hox-negative.
levels.phd:
The neural crest is a vertebrate innovation. Its gene regulatory network (GRN) has a layered structure. Border inducers (BMP, Wnt, FGF, retinoic acid) activate **neural plate border specifiers** (Pax3/7, Zic1, Msx1, Tfap2a, Dlx5). These activate **crest specifiers** (FoxD3, Snai1/2, Sox9/10, Twist, c-Myc, Id). Specifiers then drive effector genes for EMT and migration and, later, lineage programs.

Comparative work in lamprey shows that most of the GRN was present early in vertebrates. Amphioxus and tunicates have border-like cells but lack the full specifier set. Tunicate pigment cells and migratory precursors suggest a proto-crest.

**Multipotency debate.** Classic quail-chick chimera studies by **Le Douarin** mapped crest fates. They showed that environment, such as transplanted axial level, alters autonomic transmitter phenotype: adrenergic versus cholinergic. Clonal analyses by **Bronner-Fraser and Fraser**, using single-cell lineage tracing in chick trunk, found that single premigratory cells could give rise to neurons, glia and melanocytes. This supported multipotency. Likewise, **Confetti** multicolor tracing in mouse (Baggiolini et al., 2015) found that most premigratory and migratory crest cells are multipotent in vivo. Fate restriction happens late, after migration, rather than through early prespecified sublineages. Single-cell transcriptomics (Soldatov et al., 2019) described sequential binary fate decisions along the trajectory, from sensory versus autonomic/mesenchymal splits onward.

**Hox code and skeletogenic potential.** Cranial crest from the Hox-negative domain (forebrain, midbrain, r1-2) forms the facial skeleton. Ectopic **Hoxa2** expression blocks skeletogenesis, while Hoxa2 loss causes second arch duplication of first arch elements.

**Contact inhibition of locomotion** and **co-attraction** (C3a/C3aR) let crest cells migrate collectively. Planar cell polarity and N-cadherin are also involved, as Mayor's lab showed in Xenopus. **SDF1/CXCR4** chemotaxis guides crest cells, and crest cells chase placodes in a "chase-and-run" interaction.

**Schwann cell precursors** (SCPs) along nerves are a later multipotent reservoir. Adameyko et al. (2009) showed that SCPs generate many melanocytes. SCPs also contribute parasympathetic neurons, chromaffin cells and some enteric neurons, which revised the simple migration-route model.
levels.expert:
Clinically, neural crest biology explains why seemingly unrelated defects cluster together. When you see a congenital heart defect with facial anomalies or thymic problems, think crest.

**22q11.2 deletion syndrome** (TBX1 haploinsufficiency) includes several features:
- Conotruncal lesions such as interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot
- Hypocalcemia
- T-cell deficiency
- A strong lifetime risk of psychosis

TBX1 acts mainly in pharyngeal mesoderm and endoderm. It affects crest cells **non-cell-autonomously**, which illustrates that crest defects can originate in the environment.

**Hirschsprung disease** is the paradigm of oligogenic, sex-biased inheritance. RET coding and enhancer variants are the main genetic factor. The intron 1 RET enhancer variant interacts with EDNRB and other loci. Short-segment disease is more common in males. **Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis** can occur even after a pull-through operation. RET gain-of-function instead causes **MEN2**: medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from crest-derived C cells, and pheochromocytoma from chromaffin cells.

**CHARGE syndrome** (CHD7) involves both placodes and crest. **Waardenburg type 4** (SOX10, EDNRB) combines pigment defects, deafness and Hirschsprung disease. SOX10 can also add peripheral demyelination: PCWH.

**Neuroblastoma**, the most common extracranial solid tumor of infancy, arises from sympathoadrenal progenitors. Key drivers include MYCN amplification, ALK mutations and PHOX2B mutations. PHOX2B mutations also cause congenital central hypoventilation syndrome. Recent single-cell maps place tumor cells near developing chromaffin and neuroblast states. The tumor can switch between adrenergic and mesenchymal states, and the mesenchymal state is more treatment resistant. **Melanoma** reactivates crest programs, such as SOX10 and AXL-high invasive states, and this links crest EMT with metastasis.

For neurosurgeons, crest lineage matters in several ways:
- Schwannomas and neurofibromas (NF1, NF2) arise from crest-derived Schwann lineage.
- The meninges of the forebrain (telencephalic meninges) are crest-derived, while caudal meninges are mesodermal.
- **Craniofacial surgery** relies on knowing crest-mesoderm boundaries in the skull. The frontal bone is crest-derived, while the parietal bone is mesodermal. The coronal suture lies at this boundary, which is relevant to TWIST1-related craniosynostosis (Saethre-Chotzen).

Open questions include several areas:
- How adult crest-derived stem cells in skin, gut and dental pulp keep their potential
- Whether SCP-derived repair after nerve injury can be harnessed
- How the teratogen **isotretinoin** (a retinoid) disrupts cranial crest to cause ear, heart and thymic defects

keyPoints: Neural crest forms at the neural plate border and leaves by an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition
Derivatives include melanocytes, DRG neurons, autonomic and enteric neurons, Schwann cells and adrenal medulla
Cranial crest builds facial bone and cartilage; cardiac crest forms the aorticopulmonary septum
Trunk crest migrates through the anterior sclerotome, repelled by posterior ephrins and semaphorins
Hox-negative cranial crest is skeletogenic; Hoxa2 suppresses this
Neurocristopathies include Hirschsprung, Waardenburg, DiGeorge and neuroblastoma

lessons.title: Neurogenesis, Radial Glia and Cortical Layering

levels.kid:
Your brain's outer layer, the **cortex**, is like a tall apartment building with six floors. But who builds it?

Long before you were born, special helper cells called **radial glia** stretched like long ropes from the inside of your growing brain all the way to the outside. They made new brain cells, called **neurons**.

Each new neuron climbed up a rope, like a kid climbing a rope in gym class. The first neurons stopped on the lowest floors. Later neurons climbed right past them to reach higher floors. So the building grew from the inside out!

If neurons get lost and stop in the wrong place, the brain can have trouble working. That's why scientists study this climb so carefully.
levels.hs:
**Neurogenesis** means making new neurons. In the embryo, most cortical neurons are made between about weeks 6 and 20 of pregnancy, at peak rates of thousands per second.

The neurons come from a layer of stem cells lining the fluid-filled ventricles, called the **ventricular zone**. At first these cells, **neuroepithelial cells**, divide to make more copies of themselves. Then they turn into **radial glia**. A radial glial cell keeps its body near the ventricle but sends a long fiber all the way to the brain's outer surface.

Radial glia do two jobs:
- They are **stem cells** that divide to produce neurons.
- Their fibers act as **scaffolds**. Newborn neurons crawl along them, a process called **radial migration**.

The cortex is built **inside-out**. The earliest neurons settle in the deepest layer (layer 6). Each later wave migrates past the older neurons to form a more superficial layer, ending with layer 2. Layer 1 is a thin top layer formed early. A protein called **Reelin**, released by **Cajal-Retzius cells** near the surface, acts as a stop signal for migrating neurons.

Real example: in **lissencephaly** ("smooth brain"), a mutation in a migration gene such as **LIS1** leaves neurons stranded. The brain lacks normal folds, and children have severe seizures and developmental delay.
levels.college:
**From neuroepithelium to radial glia.** The early neural tube wall is a pseudostratified **neuroepithelium**. Its nuclei move up and down with the cell cycle (**interkinetic nuclear migration**): S phase happens away from the ventricle, and mitosis happens at the ventricular surface. Around the onset of neurogenesis these cells become **radial glial cells (RGCs)**. RGCs express glial markers (GLAST, BLBP, Pax6, nestin) yet act as the main neural progenitors.

**Modes of division.**
- **Symmetric proliferative** divisions expand the progenitor pool.
- **Asymmetric neurogenic** divisions yield one RGC plus a neuron or an **intermediate progenitor (IP)**.
- IPs (Tbr2+) move to the **subventricular zone (SVZ)** and divide a few times, producing neurons. This amplifies output.

**Notch signaling** keeps cells progenitors. Daughters with low Notch activity upregulate proneural genes (Neurog2, Ascl1) and differentiate, a process called lateral inhibition.

**Zones of the developing cortex** (from inside out): ventricular zone, SVZ, intermediate zone (future white matter), **subplate**, **cortical plate**, and **marginal zone** (future layer 1). The first postmitotic neurons form the **preplate**. Arriving cortical-plate neurons then split it into the marginal zone and the subplate.

**Inside-out layering.** Deep layers (6, then 5) are born first and later neurons bypass them, so layers 4, 3 and 2 form in sequence. Birth date predicts laminar fate, and fate correlates with projection: layer 6 projects to the thalamus, layer 5 to subcortical targets such as the spinal cord, and layers 2-3 to other cortical areas.

**Two migration routes.**
- **Excitatory glutamatergic** neurons arise from dorsal (pallial) progenitors and migrate **radially** on RGC fibers.
- **Inhibitory GABAergic interneurons** arise in the ventral **ganglionic eminences** (MGE, CGE) and migrate **tangentially** into the cortex.

After neurogenesis, RGCs switch to producing astrocytes and oligodendrocyte lineages. Many then transform into astrocytes.
levels.phd:
**Lineage logic.** Rakic's radial unit hypothesis (1988) proposed that RGCs link the ventricular proto-map to cortical columns. In this model, the number of radial units sets cortical surface area, and divisions per unit set thickness. Live imaging by Noctor and Kriegstein (2001) confirmed that RGCs are neurogenic. Clonal analyses (MADM, Gao et al., 2014) showed that each neurogenic RGC yields about 8-9 excitatory neurons spanning deep and superficial layers. This output is fairly deterministic, though the idea of fate-restricted subpopulations (e.g., Cux2+) remains debated.

**Temporal competence.** McConnell's heterochronic transplants showed that early progenitors are multipotent. Early cells placed in an older host could adopt upper-layer fates if transplanted before their final S phase. Late progenitors, by contrast, are restricted. A transcriptional cascade then consolidates postmitotic identity:
- **Tbr1** marks layer 6 corticothalamic neurons.
- **Fezf2/Ctip2 (Bcl11b)** drive layer 5 corticospinal identity.
- **Satb2** specifies callosal projection.
- These factors cross-repress one another. For example, Satb2 represses Ctip2, and Fezf2 loss converts corticospinal neurons to a callosal-like fate.

**Division orientation and polarity.** Spindle angle, apical endfoot inheritance, and centrosome age (the daughter that keeps the mother centriole tends to remain a progenitor) bias fate. Cell-cycle lengthening, especially of G1 (Calegari, Huttner), correlates with neurogenic commitment.

**Migration machinery.** Radial migration is multiphasic. Neurons become multipolar in the SVZ/IZ, then shift to bipolar locomotion along glia, and finish with **terminal somal translocation**. Nucleokinesis depends on a LIS1-dynein-microtubule complex linked by doublecortin (DCX). The Reelin pathway acts through VLDLR/ApoER2, Dab1 phosphorylation and Src-family kinases. In reeler mice, lamination is roughly inverted.

**Outer radial glia.** Primates possess abundant **outer RGCs (oRG)** in an expanded **outer SVZ** (Hansen et al., 2010; Fietz et al., 2010). These cells keep a basal fiber but lack an apical contact, and they divide by mitotic somal translocation. Their scaffold fans out tangentially, which favours surface expansion and gyrification. Human-specific gene **ARHGAP11B** increases basal progenitors and induces folding when expressed in mice or ferrets.
levels.expert:
**Clinical malformations of cortical development (MCDs)** map onto three stages: proliferation, migration and organization.

- **Proliferation defects**: primary microcephaly (MCPH) genes such as **ASPM**, **WDR62** and **CDK5RAP2** encode centrosome and spindle proteins. Loss shifts progenitors toward premature neurogenic divisions, which depletes the pool and shrinks surface area. Overgrowth disorders (hemimegalencephaly, focal cortical dysplasia type II) usually arise from **somatic mTOR-pathway mutations** (PIK3CA, AKT3, MTOR, DEPDC5). The size and location of the affected region reflect when and in which progenitor the mutation arose. Resected tissue may show only low-level mosaicism, so deep sequencing of brain tissue is needed because blood is often negative.
- **Migration defects**: **LIS1** (PAFAH1B1, chromosome 17p13.3; Miller-Dieker when contiguous with YWHAE) gives posterior-predominant lissencephaly. **DCX** (X-linked) gives anterior-predominant lissencephaly in males and **subcortical band heterotopia** ("double cortex") in heterozygous females through random X-inactivation. **RELN** and VLDLR variants cause lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia. **FLNA** variants cause periventricular nodular heterotopia, with neurons that never left the ventricular surface.
- **Organization defects**: polymicrogyria, linked to GPR56/ADGRG1, congenital CMV and others.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** These lesions are major causes of drug-resistant epilepsy. FCD II is a leading pathology in pediatric epilepsy surgery, and outcome tracks with complete resection. MRI clues include a transmantle sign and a blurred gray-white junction. Stereo-EEG and laser ablation are reshaping management. mTOR inhibitors are being explored as an alternative to surgery for tuberous sclerosis-related seizures.

**Pharmacology angle.** Neurogenesis and migration are teratogen targets. **Zika virus** infects RGCs and oRG via AXL and related receptors, causing microcephaly. Prenatal **valproate** exposure is linked to neurodevelopmental effects. Ethanol disrupts radial glial scaffolds and neuronal migration.

**Frontiers.** Human cortical **organoids** recapitulate oRG and the outer SVZ but lack vasculature and robust lamination. Single-cell atlases (Nowakowski 2017, and BICCN/HDBR datasets) reveal progenitor trajectories and a late "truncated RG" state. Open questions include the extent of fate restriction and how subplate transience, which is vulnerable in preterm white-matter injury, shapes connectivity.

keyPoints: Radial glia are both neural stem cells and migration scaffolds
Intermediate progenitors in the SVZ amplify neuron output
Cortex is built inside-out: deep layers first, upper layers last
Reelin from Cajal-Retzius cells signals neurons to stop migrating
Excitatory neurons migrate radially; interneurons migrate tangentially from ganglionic eminences
Defects in LIS1, DCX or RELN cause lissencephaly and heterotopia

test.q: Which cell acts both as a neural progenitor and as a guide for migrating neurons?
test.explain: Radial glia divide to make neurons, and their long basal fibers serve as scaffolds. Cajal-Retzius cells secrete Reelin but are not the scaffold.

test.q: In the developing cortex, which layer forms from the earliest-born cortical-plate neurons?
test.explain: The cortex forms inside-out, so the earliest cortical-plate neurons settle deepest, in layer 6.

test.q: Reelin, which helps neurons stop at the right position, is secreted by:
test.explain: Cajal-Retzius cells in the marginal zone release Reelin, a stop signal for migrating neurons.

test.q: Where do most cortical GABAergic interneurons originate?
test.explain: Interneurons arise in the ventral ganglionic eminences (MGE, CGE) and migrate tangentially into the cortex.

test.q: What is the main role of Tbr2-positive intermediate progenitors?
test.explain: Intermediate progenitors in the SVZ divide a few more times, which boosts neuron output.

test.q: High Notch activity in a daughter cell tends to make it:
test.explain: Notch signaling maintains progenitor status. Cells with low Notch activity express proneural genes and differentiate.

test.q: Mutations in LIS1 are a classic cause of:
test.explain: LIS1 is needed for neuronal migration. Its loss produces a smooth, poorly folded cortex (lissencephaly).

test.q: During interkinetic nuclear migration, mitosis occurs:
test.explain: Neuroepithelial and radial glial nuclei move to the ventricular (apical) surface to divide.

test.q: Layer 5 neurons characteristically send axons to:
test.explain: Layer 5 neurons project subcortically, for example to the spinal cord. Layer 6 projects to the thalamus, and layers 2-3 project to other cortex.

test.q: Neurons of the cortex are generated in an inside-___ order.
test.explain: Deep layers form first and later neurons migrate past them to more superficial layers.

test.q: What zone just above the ventricular zone contains intermediate progenitors (give the abbreviation or full name)?
test.explain: The SVZ houses Tbr2+ intermediate progenitors and, in primates, an expanded outer SVZ.

test.q: The early layer of first-born neurons, later split by the cortical plate, is the ___.
test.explain: Cortical-plate neurons split the preplate into the marginal zone and the subplate.

kidTest.q: What do radial glia cells act like for new neurons?
kidTest.explain: New neurons climb along their long fibers.

kidTest.q: How many floors does the cortex building have?
kidTest.explain: The cortex has six layers.

kidTest.q: Where do the very first neurons stop?
kidTest.explain: The first neurons stay deep, and later ones climb past them.

kidTest.q: What can happen if neurons stop in the wrong place?
choices: The brain may not work well
kidTest.explain: Neurons in the wrong spot can cause brain problems.

kidTest.q: Brain cells are called n _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Neurons are the cells that send brain signals.

advancedTest.q: In McConnell's transplants, early progenitors placed in an older host adopted upper-layer fates only when moved before their final S phase. This implies:
choices: Late progenitors can regain any deep-layer fate on request
Laminar fate is fixed at the onset of neurulation
Early progenitors are multipotent and respond to environmental cues
Reelin alone determines laminar identity after migration
advancedTest.explain: Early progenitors could be respecified by host cues, whereas late progenitors were restricted. This shows fate competence narrows over time.

advancedTest.q: Why do outer radial glia favour cortical folding in primates?
choices: Their fanning basal fibers spread neurons tangentially across more surface area
They migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences into the cortex
They secrete Reelin that inverts the order of the layers
They shorten the G1 phase so that fewer neurons are produced overall
advancedTest.explain: oRG lack apical contact and form a divergent scaffold in the expanded OSVZ, which drives surface expansion and gyrification.

advancedTest.q: A girl with a heterozygous DCX variant shows subcortical band heterotopia. The best explanation is:
choices: Random X-inactivation leaving one neuron population unable to migrate
Haploinsufficiency of Reelin signaling in the marginal zone
Somatic mTOR activation in a single late progenitor clone
Loss of centrosomal ASPM causing premature neurogenic division
advancedTest.explain: DCX is X-linked. Neurons that express the mutant allele arrest beneath the cortex and form a 'double cortex.'

advancedTest.q: A child has focal cortical dysplasia type II and blood sequencing is negative. The most appropriate interpretation is:
choices: The lesion is best explained by congenital CMV infection
A germline lissencephaly gene variant is now excluded
The dysplasia arose from tangential interneuron migration failure
A somatic mTOR-pathway variant may be confined to the brain
advancedTest.explain: FCD II usually results from brain-restricted somatic mosaicism, so resected tissue needs deep sequencing.
